title: BZAN 535: Statistical Methods
text:
Chapter Overview

Chapter 1 — Role of Statistics and Key Concepts
Introduces the role of statistics in turning data into informed decisions. Covers data types and measurement scales, populations and samples, parameters and statistics, descriptive versus inferential statistics, and the distinction between observational studies and randomized experiments. Particular attention is given to the different roles of random sampling and random assignment in supporting generalization and causal inference.


Chapter 2 — Descriptive Analysis
Develops the tools used to summarize and understand observed data. Covers measures of center, spread, and distribution shape; frequency tables; outliers; and common visualizations including histograms, boxplots, scatterplots, and bar charts. The chapter also introduces the ggplot2 framework for constructing statistical visualizations in R.


Chapter 3 — Descriptive Analytics for Time Series Data
Extends descriptive analysis to data observed over time. Introduces date and time manipulation with lubridate, time-based filtering and grouping, and visualization of temporal data. The chapter examines important time-series patterns including trend, seasonality, short-term variation, and level changes, along with techniques such as moving averages for revealing underlying patterns.


Chapter 4 — Probability Rules and Distributions
Moves from describing observed data to reasoning about uncertain outcomes. Introduces probability terminology, probability rules, conditional probability, independence, and the distinction between discrete and continuous random variables. The chapter then develops four important probability distributions—Binomial, Normal, Poisson, and Exponential—and explains how to recognize, interpret, and work with each distribution in R.

1.2 Types of Data
Categorical: qualitative values relating to characteristics.

Nomimal: categories with no meaniningful order. There’s no mathematical sense in which is greater or less than another. e.g. red, blue, green
Ordinal: categories with an order to them. Certain categories correspond to higher or lower rankings, places, etc. e.g. one star, two star, three star

Numerical

Interval: numerical values with meaningful differences but no true zero. A value of zero doesn’t neccessarily mean “none”, rather it’s just a ‘label’ similar to any other number. e.g. 0°F, 53°F
Ratio: numerical values with a true equal spacing and a true zero. In this case, a value of zero literally means “none” or “nothing there”. e.g. $0, $5 Because zero has an actual meaning, comparisons (or ratios) like “twice as much” are relevant.

1.3 Population vs. Sample

Population: entire group of interest. This is the true group in question.
Sample: the limited subset being observed.
Parameter: a description of the population. Because it involves the entire group of interest, it’s unknown (it’s impossible to actually include everyone).
Statistic: a computed description of the sample. Because the sample is only a part of the group, meaning it’s an inference that it represents the true group, it’s a predicted value.

1.6 Study Designs: Observational vs. Experimental
Suppose a company claims customers who use our app spend 40% more. Does that mean our app causes customers to spend more? Not neccessarily. Many people who download the app could already be the company’s most loyal customers. This is the problem of confounding.
Observational: observe what people already chose/did. Here, you can establish an association, but causality isn’t established merely by observing a difference.
Experiment (A/B): random assignment of subjects. This randomization helps balance other characteristics (lurking variables) between groups. Therefore, differences in outcomes can support a causal interpretation, assuming everything else in the experiement is valid.
Randomized experiments can support cause-and-effect inference, whereas observational studies do not by themselves; random sampling is separately what supports inference to a population.
Random Sampling and random assignment are not the same thing.

Random sampling answers “Can I generalize this result to the population.”.
Random Assignment answers “Can I make a causal claim?”

2.1 Overview
Raw data can be messy and overwhelming, making it difficult to interpret and work with. Descriptive analysis helps solve this problem by summarizing and exploring data in a way that turns raw numbers into patterns and insights that can be understood accurately and easily.
There are three key questions to consider:
How do we answer these questions? By examining the center, spread, and shape of the data – each of which describes a different aspect of the observations and together, helps us draw accurate conclusions about what the data is telling us.
Descriptive Analysis is organized around several key ideas:
The first three, center, spread, and shape, describe the distribution itself. Groups lets you compare distributions, while visualization is how you explore and communicate those characteristics. And all are equally important.
A Quick Example: Suppose two products both sell an average of 100 units per week:
Both products have the same average, but their weekly sales behave very differently. Knowing the average alone does not necessarily tell us what sales actually look like.
They have the same center, but very different spread.
Together, these tools help answer the key questions needed to understand a dataset before moving on to deeper analysis.

title: 2  Descriptive Analysis
text:
2.2 Center
What’s a typical value?
Center is the measure that represents the typical or central value of a dataset. It describes the location around which the data tends to lie.
There are two main measures of center: mean and median.

2.2.1 Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average of a dataset. It is calculated by adding all observations together and dividing by the number of observations.
\(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum{x_i}}{n}\)
Pros:

Uses every observation in dataset.
Easy to calculate and interpret.

Cons:

Sensitive to outliers.
Can be misleading for highly skewed distributions.



2.2.2 Median
Median is the middle value of a dataset after the observations have been ordered. It is more robust to outliers than the mean. For a odd number of observations, sort the data and take the middle value. For an even number of observations (i.e. two middle values) take the two middle values and average them.
Pros:

Robust to outliers and extreme values.
Often better represents the center of skewed data.

Cons:

Does not incorportate the magnitude of every observation the same way the mean does.
Can ignore meaningful differences in the values away from the middle.

title: 2  Descriptive Analysis
text:
2.3 Spread
How much do values vary?
Spread describes how much the observations in a dataset vary or differ from one another. In other words, it tells us how dispersed the data is around its center.

2.3.1 Range
The range measures the distance between the smallest and largest observations.
\(\text{range} = \text{maximum} - \text{minimum}\)
Pros:

Extremely simple to calculate or understand.

Cons:

Only considers two observations – the largest and smallest – so it is highly sensitive to outliers.



2.3.2 IQR
The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the observations. In other words, how much do the middle 50% of values span? Because it ignores the extreme ends, it’s resilient to outliers.
\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)
\(Q_1\) is the 25th percentile. \(Q_3\) is the 75h percentile.
Conceptually, IQR looks at: \[
\underbrace{\text{lowest 25\%}}_{\phantom{x}}
\quad|\quad
\underbrace{Q_1\; \longleftrightarrow\; Q_3}_{\text{middle 50\%}}
\quad|\quad
\underbrace{\text{highest 25\%}}_{\phantom{x}}
\]
Pros:

Robust to outliers.

Cons:

Does not incorportate all observations.



2.3.3 Variance
Variance measures how spread out observations are around the mean using their squared deviations from the mean. The deviations are squared so that negative and positive deviations do not cancel each other out.
To calculate:

Find the mean.
Find how far each observation is from the mean.
Square each difference.
Add the squared differences.
Divide by n-1.

\(s^2 = \frac{\sum{(x_i - \bar{x})^2}}{n-1}\)
Pros:

Uses every observation in the dataset.
Measures spread specifically around the mean, so it pairs naturally with the mean.

Cons: - Expressed in squared units, meaning it is less intuitive.


2.3.4 Standard Deviation
Standard Deviation is the square root of the variance. It allows for an interpretable scale of how much values differ from mean by putting variance back into original units.
\(s = \sqrt{s^2}\)
Pros:

Easy to interpret.

Cons:

Its magnitude depends on the scale of the data and can be misleading when comparing two variables of different scales.
Sensitive to outliers.



2.3.5 Coefficient of Variation
The Coefficient of Variation measures the standard deviation relative to the mean. In other words, it tells you how large the standard deviation is compared to the mean (how big is distance based on mean).
\(\text{CV} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\bar{x}}\)
Pros:

Can accurately compare spread of variables with different scales.

Cons:

Not useful when mean is zero, because you cannot divide by zero.
Can be sensitive to outliers.

title: 2  Descriptive Analysis
text:
2.4 Shape
What does the distribution look like?
Shape describes the overall pattern or form of a distribution. It helps us understand how observations are distributed around the center, including whether the data is symmetric, skewed, or contains outliers.

2.4.1 Symmetric
A symmetric distribution has approximately the same shape on both sides of its center. Neither side has a substantially longer tail than the other.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median tend to be relatively close.


2.4.2 Right Skewed
A right-skewed distribution has a long tail extending to the right, toward larger values.
A relatively small number of large observations stretch the distribution to the right and can pull the mean upward.
Typically: \(\text{right skewed} \rightarrow \text{mean}>\text{median}\)


2.4.3 Left Skewed
A left-skewed distribution has a long tail extending to the left, toward smaller values.
A relatively small number of small observations stretch the distribution to the left and can pull the mean downward.
Left tail \(\rightarrow\) mean pulled left \(\rightarrow\) Mean < Median Right tail \(\rightarrow\) mean pulled right \(\rightarrow\) Mean > Median


2.4.4 Outliers
An outlier is an observation that is unusually far from the rest of the data.
The IQR rule can be used to identify potential outliers.
\(\text{lower bound}=Q_1-1.5(IQR)\)
\(\text{upper bound}=Q_3+1.5(IQR)\)
If the observation is outside of these bounds it can be flagged as a potential outlier.
An outlier should not automatically be deleted. It is important to investigate its cause first. For example, an extreme observation could represent a data-entry error, a legitimate unusual observation, or a measurement/unit issue.

2.6.1 Histograms
A histogram shows the distribution of a single quantitative variable by grouping numerical values into intervals called bins and showing how many observations fall into each bin.
Useful for identifying:

Shape of a distribution
Skewness
Modes or peaks
Gaps

The bin width determines how wide each interval is and therefore how much detail the histogram shows

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)








Use when: You want to see what the distribution of one quantitative variable looks like.


2.6.2 Boxplots
A boxplot provides a compact summary of the distribution of a quantitative variable using the five-number summary: \(\text{Min},\ Q_1,\ \text{Median},\ Q_3,\ \text{Max}\)
It is useful for examining:

Center
Spread
Skewness
Potential outliers
Differences between groups

Boxplots are especially useful when you want to compare distributions across categories.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
    geom_boxplot()








Use when: You want to examine or compare the distributions of quantitative data, particularly across groups.


2.6.3 Scatterplots
A scatterplot shows the relationship between two quantitative variables. Each point represents one observation.
Useful for identifying:

Direction — positive or negative relationship
Strength — how closely the variables are related
Form — linear, nonlinear, etc.
Outliers


ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
    geom_point()








Use when: You want to know whether two quantitative variables are related.


2.6.4 Bar Charts
A bar chart displays the counts or proportions of categories for a categorical variable. It is essentially the graphical version of a frequency table.
The categories are represented by bars, and the height of each bar represents its count.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
    geom_bar()








Use when: You want to compare counts or proportions across categories.


2.6.5 Pie Charts
A pie chart displays proportions of a whole as slices of a circle. Larger slices represent larger proportions.
Pie charts work best when there are only a small number of categories. Similar-sized slices can be difficult to compare visually, so a bar chart is often easier to interpret.

mtcars |>
    count(cyl) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = "", y = n, fill = factor(cyl))) +
    geom_col(width = 1) +
    coord_polar(theta = "y")








Use when: You want to show how a small number of categories make up a whole.

title: 2  Descriptive Analysis
text:
2.7 ggplot2
ggplot2 is a data visualization package in R built by combining data, aesthetics, and layers.
data + aesthetics + layers
Data = what you’re plotting aes() = which variables control visual properties geom_*() = how the observations are drawn scale_*() = how values are displayed facet_*() = split into groups labs() = titles and labels theme_*() = appearance

2.7.1 Aesthetics
Aesthetics, specified with aes(), determine how variables in the data are mapped to visual properties of the graph.
Common aesthetics include:

x — horizontal position
y — vertical position
color — color
size — size
shape — shape
alpha — transparency


ggplot(mtcars, aes(
    x = wt,
    y = mpg,
    color = factor(cyl)
))










2.7.2 Layers
Layers determine how the data is actually displayed. They are usually added with geom_*() functions using +.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
    geom_point()








Examples include:
geom_point() geom_histogram() geom_boxplot() geom_col()


2.7.3 Mapping vs. Setting
Mapping means a visual property varies according to a variable in the data. Put it inside aes()

ggplot(mtcars, aes(
    x = wt,
    y = mpg,
    color = factor(cyl)
)) +
    geom_point()








Different household-size categories receive different colors.
Setting means giving a visual property one fixed value. Put it outside aes()

ggplot(mtcars, aes(
    x = wt,
    y = mpg
    )) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue")








Now every point is steel blue.


2.7.4 Scales
Scales control how mapped data values are displayed, such as transforming or formatting an axis.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_y_log10()








scale_y_log10() cisplays the y-axis on a logarithmic scale.


2.7.5 Facets
Facets split one visualization into separate plots for different groups.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(~ cyl)








Instead of showing every household-size group on one graph, you get a separate panel for each household size.


2.7.6 Labels
labs() controls the descriptive text on the visualization:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(
        title = "Vehicle Weight vs. Fuel Efficiency",
        subtitle = "1973–74 Motor Trend road tests",
        x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
        y = "Miles per Gallon",
        color = "Cylinders"
    )










2.7.7 Themes
Themes control the overall appearance of the plot rather than the underlying data.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
    geom_point() +
    theme_minimal()

title: 3  Descriptive Analytics for Time Series Data
text:
3.1 Overview
For descriptive analysis, the focus was on questions such as: What is typical? How spread out is the data? What shape does the distribution have? With time series data, an additional question becomes important: When did it happen?
Time series data is a sequence of observations collected or recorded at successive points in time. Because observations are ordered chronologically, time series data provides a dynamic view of how a variable changes over time, rather than a static snapshot.
Suppose a CFO says” “Sales dropped 15% from Q3 to Q4.”
That number by itself doesn’t necessarily mean the business suddently got worse. Maybe sales normally decline from Q3 to Q4 and this is just a regular reoccurring observation.
With time series data, there are three things to be distinguished:

title: 3  Descriptive Analytics for Time Series Data
text:
Chronological order: Observations occur sequentially over time so ordering of the data matters.
Time index: Each oberservation is associated with a specific point in time.
Dependence over time: Earlier and later observations may be related, meaning observations may not be independent.
Temporal patterns: The ordering of observations allows patterns like trend, seasonality, and short term variation to be identified.





Trend \(\rightarrow\) Is there a long-term upward/downward movement?
Seasonality \(\rightarrow\) Does a pattern repeat at regular intervals?
Noise \(\rightarrow\) Is a movement just short-term random variation?
Level Change \(\rightarrow\) Did the series actually shift to a different level?

title: 3  Descriptive Analytics for Time Series Data
text:
3.2 Working with Lubridate
Why do dates matter in analytics? Dates can be used for several things, for example:

Time aware filtering (e.g. time based filtering), time aware grouping (group a time period), and trend/seasonality detection.
Aligning events (comparing before and afters).
Preparing for forecasting.

Dates need to actually be dates! A date stored as text like:
'2025-08-21'
is much different from an R Date object actually representing August 21, 2025. The main package used when working with dates is lubridate.

3.2.1 Parsing Dates
Parsing dates is the process of converting raw string dates to an actual date/time object, which can then be converted into useful time components. Raw string dates may not always be written in a consistent way, therefore different functions are used based on what the text format is.

ymd() when string = YEAR \(\rightarrow\) MONTH \(\rightarrow\) DAY
mdy() when string = MONTH \(\rightarrow\) DAY \(\rightarrow\) YEAR
dmy() when string = DAY \(\rightarrow\) MONTH \(\rightarrow\) YEAR
ymd_hms() when string = YEAR \(\rightarrow\) MONTH \(\rightarrow\) DAY : HH:MM:SS

Example:

ymd("2025-08-21")

[1] "2025-08-21"

mdy("08/21/2025")

[1] "2025-08-21"

dmy("21-Aug-2025")

[1] "2025-08-21"

ymd_hms("2025-08-21 14:30:00")

[1] "2025-08-21 14:30:00 UTC"


Once the date is in the correct format, R can extract pieces:

year(x) = extract year
month(x) = extract month
quarter(x) = extract quarter
wday(x) = extract weekday
hour(x) = extract hour
isoweek(x) = extract week number of year


x <- ymd_hms("2025-08-21 14:30:00")
x

[1] "2025-08-21 14:30:00 UTC"

year(x)

[1] 2025

month(x)

[1] 8

quarter(x)

[1] 3

wday(x)

[1] 5

hour(x)

[1] 14

isoweek(x)

[1] 34


Esssentially the process is raw date string → actual date/time object → useful time components
Dates can also be created from combining variables that already exist. For example if you have year = 2025 and month = 8 you can construct an actual date.
make_date() use when year/month columns exist because it avoids rounding problems associated with fractional-year representations

# Before: year and month are separate variables
txhousing |>
    select(year, month) |>
    head(2)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
   year month
  <int> <int>
1  2000     1
2  2000     2

# Create an actual date from year and month
TX <- txhousing |>
    mutate(
        date_actual = make_date(
            year = year,
            month = month,
            day = 1
        )
    )

# After: year and month have been combined into a date
TX |>
    select(year, month, date_actual) |>
    head(2)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
   year month date_actual
  <int> <int> <date>     
1  2000     1 2000-01-01 
2  2000     2 2000-02-01 




3.2.2 Calendar Arithmetic
Leap years can screw up calculation of dates. For example ymd("2024-02-29") is a leap year. If you subtract five years you’d get 2019-02-29 which doesn’t exist.

d1 <- ymd("2024-02-29")

lubridate has calendar awareness operators:

d1 %m-% years(5)

[1] "2019-02-28"

ymd("2023-01-31") %m+% months(1)

[1] "2023-02-28"

For time-series data, the standard visualization is a line chart.

4.1 Overview
This section marks the transition from describing observed data to reasoning about uncertain outcomes. In earlier sections, the focus was on concepts such as center, spread, shape, and trends. Now we extend that framework by asking: “What could happen, and how likely is each outcome?” Answering this requires more than descriptive statistics. It requires looking at probabilities and probability distributions.

title: 4  Probability Rules and Distributions
text:
4.2 Probability

4.2.1 Probability Terminology
A probability is a number from 0 to 1 describing how likely an event is.








Term
Meaning
Example




Experiment
Random process
Send a marketing email


Outcome
One possible result
Customer clicks


Event
One or more outcomes you’re interested in
Customer engages


Sample Space
All possible outcomes
{Click, Open, Ignore, Unsubscribe}





4.2.2 Basic Probability Rules

4.2.2.1 Complement Rule
The complement rule finds the probability that an event does not happen.
\[
P(A^c)=1-P(A)
\] If event A happens with probability P(A), its complement, written A^c, means “not A.”
For example:
If there’s a 20% chance of clicking: \(P(\text{No click})=1-.20=.80\)


4.2.2.2 Addition Rule
The addition rule finds the probability that event A OR event B occurs.
\[P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B) - P(A)\]
However, that only works if Event A and Event B can occur simultaneously.
If A and B are Mututally Exclusive: \[P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)\]
For example:
Suppose:

\(P(\text{opens email})=0.50\)
\(P(\text{clicks link})=0.20\)
\(P(\text{opens AND clicks})=0.15\)

Then:
\(P(\text{opens OR clicks})=0.50+0.20-0.15=0.55\)
Note: if mutually exclusive: \(P(\text{opens OR clicks})=0.50+0.20=0.70\)


4.2.2.3 Multiplication
The multiplication rule finds the probability that event A AND event B occur.
If A and B are Dependent Events:
\[P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B\mid A)\]
If A and B are Independent Events:
\[P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)\]



4.2.3 Conditional Probability
Conditional Probability is the probability an event occurs given another has occured (i.e. probability of Event A given Event B occurred)
\[P(A\mid B)\]

title: 4  Probability Rules and Distributions
text:
4.3 Distributions

4.3.1 Binomial Distribution
A binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number trials, where each trial has two possible outcomes: success or failure. Each trial is independent and the probability of success remains constant.
Discrete
\[X\sim\text{Binomial}(n,p)\]

\(X \rightarrow \text{a discrete random variable}\)
\(n \rightarrow \text{number of independent trials}\)
\(p \rightarrow \text{probability of success}\)

dbinom(k, n, p) probability exactly k successes pbinom(k, n, p) probability less than or equal to k successes


4.3.2 Normal Distribution
A normal distribution models a continuous random variable with values that are distributed symmetrically around a mean, with values closer to the mean occurring more frequently than values farther from the mean.
mean = median = mode
Continuous
\[X\sim\text{Normal}(\mu,\sigma)\]

\(X \rightarrow \text{a continuous random variable}\)
\(\mu \rightarrow \text{mean}\)
\(\sigma \rightarrow \text{standard deviation}\)

dnorm(x, mu, sigma) height of the curve at 100, not probability (continuous variable) pnorm(x, mu, sigma) area to the left of 100, which is a probability

Z-score

How many standard deviations away from mean.


\(z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\)
Empirical Rule

68% are within one standard deviation away from mean 
95% are within two standard deviations away from mean 
99.7% are within two standard deviations away from mean 

Three ways to assess whether data are approximately normally distributed

Histogram: Shows the shape of the data (roughly symmetric, bell-shaped)
Q-Q plot: Compares observed data to what we’d expect from a normal distribution (points roughly follow a straight line)
Shapiro-Wilk test: Formal hypothesis test for normality (p > 0.05: do not reject normality)



4.3.3 Poisson Distribution
A Poisson distribution models the number of times an event occurs within a fixed interval of time.
expected number of events (\(\lambda\)) = mean = variance
Discrete
\[X\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda)\]

\(X \rightarrow \text{number of events in the interval}\)
\(\lambda \rightarrow \text{average number of events per interval}\)

Function
Calculates
Meaning

dpois(k, lambda) exactly k events
ppois(k, lambda) k or fewer events


Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test

A chi-square goodness-of-fit test compares the observed event counts to the expected counts under a Poisson distribution.



\(H_0\): The data are consistent with a Poisson distribution.
\(H_A\): The data are not consistent with a Poisson distribution.
\(p > 0.05\): Fail to reject \(H_0\) → data are reasonably consistent with Poisson.
\(p < 0.05\): Reject \(H_0\) → evidence that the data do not fit a Poisson distribution.


Overdispersion Check

For a Poisson distribution, the mean and variance should be approximately equal.


\[
\frac{\text{Variance}}{\text{Mean}} \approx 1
\]


4.3.4 Exponential Distribution
An exponential distribution models the time between events in a Poisson process. While the Poisson distribution models how many events occur in an interval, the exponential distribution models how long until the next event occurs.
Continuous
\[
T \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda)
\]

\(T \rightarrow \text{waiting time until the next event}\)
\(\lambda \rightarrow \text{average rate at which events occur}\)
dexp(t, rate = lambda) density at \(t\)
pexp(t, rate = lambda) probability the event occurs within time \(t\)
qexp(p, rate = lambda) waiting time associated with cumulative probability \(p\)
rexp(n, rate = lambda) generate exponential waiting times

Exponential is memoryless: meaning independent events don’t remember what has already happened. What has occurred doesn’t impact what is to come.

title: 5  One-Parameter Statistical Inference
text:
5.1 Overview
So far, the focus has been on describing observed data and modeling uncertainty. Descriptive statistics summarize the data we actually observe. Probability distributions describe how uncertain outcomes behave. Statistical inference takes the next step: what can a sample tell us about a population we cannot fully observe?
Suppose a company reports:
That number may sound precise, but suppose it came from a sample of 2,500 households rather than every household. The sample mean \(\bar{x} = 1793\) is known, but the population mean \(\mu\) is unknown.
The goal of statistical inference is to use the observed sample statistic to learn about the unknown population parameter, while explicitly accounting for sampling uncertainty.
The general process is:
\[\text{Population} \rightarrow \text{Sample} \rightarrow \text{Statistic} \rightarrow \text{Inference about Parameter}\]
There are two major tools for doing this:
Before either one works, however, we need to understand sampling variability.

title: 5  One-Parameter Statistical Inference
text:
Average household spending last month was $1,793.







Confidence intervals

Estimate a population parameter

Hypothesis tests

Evaluate a claim about a population parameter

title: 5  One-Parameter Statistical Inference
text:
5.2 Sampling
A sample is a subset of a population that you actually observe or collect data from. The goal is usually to use information from the sample to learn about the population. This connects to statistics vs. parameters (see Section 1).

Bias

The estimate is consistently off from the true value (population) in a particular way, likely caused by poor design.

Variance

Sample-to-sample variation that occurs naturally, even with good design. Decreases as \(n\), the number of observations, decreases.


Common sources of bias:

Coverage bias \(\rightarrow\) Some members of the population have little or no chance of being included because the sampling method does not adequately cover the population.
Selection bias \(\rightarrow\) The method used to select participants systematically favors certain types of people over others.
Nonresponse bias \(\rightarrow\) People who do not respond differ systematically from those who do respond in a way related to the question being studied.

\[\boxed{\text{Coverage}=\text{Who can be reached}} \boxed{\text{Selection}=\text{Who gets selected}} \boxed{\text{Nonresponse}=\text{Who actually responds}}\]
Sampling Methods

Simple Random Sampling

equal chance for everyone.

Stratified Sampling

divide into groups, then sample from EACH group.

Cluster

divide into groups, randomly choose SOME groups, then sample within those selected groups

Systematic

every \(k\)-th unit after a random start

title: 5  One-Parameter Statistical Inference
text:
5.3 Sampling Distribution and the CLT

5.3.1 Sampling Distribution and SE
Suppose you drew a different random sample of 2,500 households and recomputed the average spend each time, 1000 times. What would the distributions of those averages be? How would that be different from the the distribution of the raw values themselves?
The sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic (e.g., \(\bar{X}\)) across all possible repeated samples of the same size from a population.

Center

tells us where the statistic tends to fall and whether it is centered on the true population parameter.


If \(E(\bar X) = \mu\), \(\bar{X}\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu\), the true value (in this case the mean).

Spread

tells us the precision of the statistic across samples.


For sample mean: \(SE(\bar{X})=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\) where smaller SE (standard error) means less sample-to-sample variability.
Standard Error measures how much a statistic would typically vary from sample to sample.


5.3.2 Central Limit Theorem
The central limit theorem says as the sample size, \(n\), gets larger, the sampling distribution of the sample mean, \(bar{X}\) becomes approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the population distribution.
*Rule of thumb, \(n \geq 30\) is often “large enough” though more skew may require a larger \(n\).
The CLT allows us to build confidence intervals and hypothesis tests even when the raw data isn’t normal.

title: 5  One-Parameter Statistical Inference
text:
5.4 Inference for the Mean
When trying to estimate the mean of a population, we use a point estimate for the mean \(\bar{X}\).
A point estimate is a single value calculated from a sample that is used to estimate an unknown population parameter.
When doing interference, the true standard deviation, \(\sigma\), is unknown. Because of this, we use the t-distribution to model it (\(t_{n-1}\)).
\[\bar{X} \pm t_{\alpha/2,\;n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\] Where:

\(\bar{X} \rightarrow\) point estimate of 
\(t_{\alpha/2,n-1} \rightarrow\) critical t-value with n-1 degrees of freedom (desired confidence level)
\(\frac{s}{\sqrt n} \rightarrow\) standard error
\(t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n} \rightarrow\) margin of error


Interpretation: the procedure covers \(\mu\) in \(100(1-\alpha)%\) of repeated samples. e.g. We are 95% confident that the mean is within…


curve(
  dt(x, df = 9),
  from = -4,
  to = 4,
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "t",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "t Distribution"
)









5.4.1 t vs z
A t-statistic is like a z-statistic when the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and must be estimated using \(s\).









\(z\)
\(t\)




Distribution
Standard normal \(N(0,1)\)
\(t\)-distribution


Population SD \(\sigma\)
Known
Unknown


Standard error
\(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
\(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Degrees of freedom
None

Shape
Normal
Normal-like, heavier tails


Critical value for 95%
\(1.96\)
Depends on \(df\)


Common use for means
Less common
Most common



As \(n\) gets larger, the difference between \(t\) and \(z\) becomes smaller and eventually negligible because \(s\) becomes a more precise estimate of \(\sigma\).

Helpful Definitions:

Distribution

a z-statistic follows the standard normal distribution \(N(0,1)\). A t-statistic follows a \(t-distribution\).

Population SD \(\sigma\)

if the true population SD \(\sigma\) is known, use \(z\). If \(\sigma\) is unknown, estimate it with the sample SD \(s\) and use \(t\).

Standard error

measures how much \(\bar{X}\) varies across samples. With \(z\), \(SE=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\). With \(t\), because \(\sigma\) is unknown, we estimate it with \(SE=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\).

Degrees of freedom

\(z\) doesn’t need degrees of freedom because \(\sigma\) is known. \(t\) uses \(df=n-1\), which accounts for estimating variability using the sample.

Shape

both are bell-shaped and centered at 0. The \(t-distribution\) has heavier tails because estimating \(\sigma\) with \(s\) introduces additional uncertainty.

Critical value for 95%

for \(z\), the middle 95% is always between -1.96 and +1.96; for t, it depends on \(n\) (\(n-1\)).

Common use for means

knowing the true population \(\sigma\) is uncommon, so \(z\) is less common for inference about means. Usually \(\sigma\) is unknown, making \(t\) the standard choice.




5.4.2 Hypothesis Testing for the Mean
\(H_0 \rightarrow\) the Null Hypothesis: the baseline/default claim. \(H_a \rightarrow\) the Alternative Hypothesis: what we are looking for evidence of (represents a difference/effect/change from null)
Steps: hypothesis \(\rightarrow\) significance level \(\alpha\) test statistic \(\rightarrow\) \(p-value\) \(\rightarrow\) decision \(\rightarrow\) conclusion

\(\alpha\) = probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true \(H_0\))
\(\beta\) = probability of a Type II error (failing to reject a false \(H_0\))
\(\text{Power} = 1-\beta\) is the probability that a hypothesis test correctly detects a real effect.










Error
What Happens
Probability
Think




Type I
Reject a true \(H_0\)
\(\alpha\)
False positive


Type II
Fail to reject a false \(H_0\)
\(\beta\)
False negative




5.4.2.1 One-Sided t-Test and Power
A one-sided t-test tests whether a population mean is larger than or smaller than a hypothesized value, depending on the specified direction.

Right-tailed: \(H_A: \mu > \mu_0\)
Left-tailed: \(H_A: \mu < \mu_0\)

Reject \(H_0\) when: \(p\text{-value} \leq \alpha\)

title: 5  One-Parameter Statistical Inference
text:
5.5 Inference for a Proportion
Inference for a proportion uses essentially the same inference framework as inference for a mean, but the population parameter changes.
For means, the population parameter is: \(\mu = \text{population mean}\)
For proportions, the population parameter is: \(p = \text{population proportion}\)

Same inference process, new parameter.










Mean \(\mu\)
Proportion \(p\)




Point Estimate
\(\bar{X}\)
\(\hat{p}\)


Standard Error
\(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)
\(\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}\)


Reference Distribution
\(t_{n-1}\)
\(z\) (Normal)


Confidence Interval
\(\bar{X} \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1} \cdot SE\)
\(\hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot SE\)


Test Statistic (\(H_0\))
\(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}\)
\(\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}\)



For proportion inference, each observation is a binary outcome:
\(X_i = \begin{cases}1 & \text{success} \\ 0 & \text{failure} \end{cases}\)
Each observation follows a Bernoulli distribution:
\(X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) where \(p\) is the true population probability or proportion of success.

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
6.1 Overview
Lecture 5 introduced inference for one population parameter.
For example, we could ask whether a population mean differs from some benchmark:
\[
H_0:\mu=\mu_0
\]
Now suppose we have two sets of measurements and want to compare their means.
Examples include:
Before choosing a statistical test, the most important question is:
If observations can be meaningfully linked one-to-one, we have paired data.
If no meaningful one-to-one relationship exists, we instead have independent samples.
This distinction determines how the data should be analyzed.

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
Customer spending before vs. after joining a loyalty program
Store sales before vs. after a layout change
Measurements from matched treatment and control stores
Measurements from twins or other naturally matched subjects



Are the observations in the two conditions independent, or are they meaningfully connected?

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
7.1 What Creates a Pair?
A pair exists when an observation in one condition can be meaningfully linked to exactly one observation in another condition.
Common forms of pairing include:

7.1.1 Repeated Measurements
The same observational unit is measured twice.
Examples:

Same customer before and after a program
Same employee before and after training
Same store before and after a redesign



7.1.2 Natural Pairs
Different observational units have a meaningful natural relationship.
Examples:

Identical twins
Siblings
Matched geographic locations



7.1.3 Matched Pairs
Researchers intentionally match similar observational units before comparing treatments.
Examples:

Match two stores with similar historical sales
Match customers with similar demographics
Match patients with similar baseline characteristics

One member of each pair may then receive one treatment while the other receives another.
crumbs: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
section: 12.1 Standard Error of the Mean Difference
text:
12.1 Standard Error of the Mean Difference
Let:
\[
s_d
\]
represent the sample standard deviation of the differences.
Then:
\[
SE(\bar{d})
=
\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
where:
\(n\) = number of pairs
Notice that \(n\) is not the total number of individual measurements.
If there are 15 pairs, then:
\[
n=15
\]
even though there are:
\[
30
\]
individual measurements.
crumbs: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
12.2 Paired t-Test Statistic
To test:
\[
H_0:\mu_d=0
\]
the test statistic is:
\[
\boxed{
t=
\frac{\bar{d}-0}
{s_d/\sqrt{n}}
}
\]
More generally:
\[
t=
\frac{\bar{d}-\mu_{d,0}}
{s_d/\sqrt{n}}
\]
The degrees of freedom are:
\[
df=n-1
\]
The test statistic tells us:

How many standard errors the observed mean difference lies from the value specified by the null hypothesis.

A large absolute value of \(t\) means the observed mean difference is far from the null value relative to the amount of sampling uncertainty.
crumbs: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
13.1 Paired t-Test in R
If the differences have already been calculated:

t.test(
    pairs$Difference,
    mu = 0
)

This is simply a one-sample t-test on the differences.
The example produces approximately:
\[
t=3.23
\]
\[
df=14
\]
\[
p=0.006
\]
and a 95% confidence interval of approximately:
\[
(0.067,\ 0.331)
\]
Because:
\[
p<0.05
\]
we reject:
\[
H_0:\mu_d=0
\]
The data provide evidence that the population mean difference is not zero.
crumbs: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
13.2 Using paired = TRUE
R can also calculate the differences internally.
For example:

t.test(
    pairs$Unaffected,
    pairs$Affected,
    paired = TRUE
)

This performs the same conceptual analysis:
\[
d_i
=
\text{Unaffected}_i
-
\text{Affected}_i
\]
followed by a one-sample t-test on those differences.

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
16.1 Step 1: Match Similar Units
Before treatment assignment, form pairs of similar stores using pre-experiment characteristics such as:

Baseline sales
Store size
Customer traffic
Neighborhood characteristics

The goal is to make the stores within each pair as comparable as possible before the treatment occurs.

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
16.2 Step 2: Randomize Within Each Pair
Within each matched pair:

Randomly assign one store to treatment
Randomly assign the other to control

Randomization remains important.
Matching improves comparability and precision, while random assignment supports causal inference.

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
section: 16.3 Step 3: Calculate One Difference Per Pair
text:
16.3 Step 3: Calculate One Difference Per Pair
For pair \(i\), calculate:
\[
d_i
=
\text{Sales}_{\text{endcap},i}
-
\text{Sales}_{\text{control},i}
\]
Then analyze:
\[
d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_n
\]
and test:
\[
H_0:\mu_d=0
\]
The key distinction is:

Matching improves precision. Random assignment supports causality.

They serve different purposes.

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
section: 17.1 Independence Within a Pair Is Not Required
text:
17.1 Independence Within a Pair Is Not Required
The two observations within a pair do not need to be independent.
In fact, the reason for using a paired analysis is usually that they are related.
For example:
\[
(\text{Before}_i,\text{After}_i)
\]
for the same store are naturally connected.
That relationship is exactly what the paired analysis preserves.
What needs to be independent is:
\[
d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_n
\]
across separate pairs.
crumbs: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
17.2 Normality Applies to the Differences
A paired t-test does not require both original variables to be Normally distributed.
You do not separately need:
\[
X\sim N
\]
and:
\[
Y\sim N
\]
Instead, the relevant quantity is:
\[
D=X-Y
\]
For small samples, we want the distribution of:
\[
d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_n
\]
to be reasonably consistent with a Normal distribution and free of severe outliers.
Therefore:

Check the differences, not the two original columns separately.

title: 6  Comparing Two Population Means: Paired Samples
text:
25.1 Examples

25.1.1 Same Customers Before and After
Monthly spending is recorded for the same customers before and after they join a loyalty program.
Paired
Each customer’s before measurement is linked to that same customer’s after measurement.



25.1.2 Randomized Website Experiment
One group of customers sees the current website.
A different group sees a redesigned website.
Independent
There is no one-to-one correspondence between customers in the two groups.



25.1.3 Matched Stores
Treatment stores are intentionally matched with similar control stores before an experiment.
Paired
Each treatment store has a specific matched control store.



25.1.4 Different Orders Across Months
Delivery times from one group of orders this month are compared with a different group of orders last month.
Independent
An order this month does not correspond to one specific order from last month.

7.1 Overview
Lecture 6 considered situations where observations from two conditions were meaningfully linked.
For paired data, each pair produced one difference:
\[
d_i=X_{1i}-X_{2i}

and the analysis became a one-sample inference problem involving:
\[
\mu_d

Suppose we want to compare:

These are independent samples.
Instead of analyzing within-pair differences, we compare the two sample means:
\[
\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2
\]
to learn about the difference between the two population means:
\[
\boxed{\mu_1-\mu_2}
\]
The major distinction is:

text:
Spending by homeowners vs. renters
Sales of national-brand vs. private-brand products
Customers assigned to Website A vs. Website B
Employees receiving one training program vs. employees receiving another









Paired samples compare within-pair differences. Independent samples compare two separate group means.

title: 7  Comparing Two Population Means: Independent Samples
text:
9.1 Paired Samples
Observations are paired when each observation in one condition has a meaningful one-to-one connection with an observation in the other condition.
Examples:

Same customer before and after treatment
Same store before and after a redesign
Identical twins
Matched treatment and control stores

Each pair produces:
\[
d_i=X_{1i}-X_{2i}
\]
and inference is performed on:
\[
\mu_d
\]
crumbs: 7  Comparing Two Population Means: Independent Samples

title: 7  Comparing Two Population Means: Independent Samples
text:
9.2 Independent Samples
Samples are independent when the groups contain different observational units and there is no meaningful one-to-one link between observations across groups.
Examples:

20 randomly selected men vs. 20 independently selected women
Homeowners vs. renters
National-brand products vs. private-brand products
Customers assigned to two different website versions

Each observational unit contributes to only one group.
The parameter of interest is:
\[
\boxed{\mu_1-\mu_2}
\]

title: 7  Comparing Two Population Means: Independent Samples
text:
10.1 Example: Taste Test
Suppose a company wants to compare mean taste ratings for Coke and Pepsi.

10.1.1 Independent-Samples Design
Randomly assign participants to one of two groups:

Group 1 tastes Coke
Group 2 tastes Pepsi

Each participant tastes only one product.
The groups are independent.


10.1.2 Paired Design
Every participant tastes both Coke and Pepsi.
Each participant provides:
\[
(\text{Coke Rating}_i,\text{Pepsi Rating}_i)
\]
The observations are paired because both ratings come from the same person.
The two designs answer similar questions but use different information.
The paired design controls for individual differences in taste preferences because each participant acts as their own comparison.
However, the study would need to prevent order effects.
For example, tasting Coke first might affect a participant’s Pepsi rating.
A common solution would be to randomize which product each participant tastes first.

title: 7  Comparing Two Population Means: Independent Samples
text:
15.1 Welch’s Test in R
R uses Welch’s method by default when performing an independent two-sample t-test.

t.test(
    outcome ~ group,
    data = my_data
)

For example:

t.test(
    spending ~ homeowner_desc,
    data = households
)

Unless otherwise specified, t.test() does not assume equal population variances.
This makes Welch’s method the standard default when there is no strong reason to assume that the two population variances are equal.

title: 7  Comparing Two Population Means: Independent Samples
text:
16.1 Pooled Test in R
Unlike Welch’s method, pooling must be requested explicitly:

t.test(
    outcome ~ group,
    data = my_data,
    var.equal = TRUE
)

The argument:

var.equal = TRUE

tells R to assume equal population variances.

30.6 Step 6: Quantify the Uncertainty
Using Welch’s method:
\[
SE(\hat{\Delta})
=
\sqrt{
\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}
+
\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}
}
\]

\[
\hat{\Delta}
\pm

\]

\[

    data = my_data

    outcome ~ group,
    data = my_data,
    var.equal = TRUE
)

text:
13.1 Confidence Interval
When constructing the confidence interval, we are not assuming the population proportions are equal.
Therefore, we estimate their variability separately using:
\[
\hat{p}_1
\]
and:
\[
\hat{p}_2
\]
The standard error is:
\[
SE_{CI}
=
\sqrt{
\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1}
+
\frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}
}
\]

title: 8  Inference for Categorical Data
text:
13.2 Hypothesis Test
Under the null hypothesis:
\[
H_0:p_1=p_2
\]
we are explicitly assuming that both groups share one common population proportion.
Therefore, we estimate that common proportion using the pooled sample proportion:
\[
\boxed{
\hat{p}_{pool}
=
\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}
}
\]
The hypothesis-test standard error uses:
\[
\hat{p}_{pool}
\]
because the test asks:

If the null hypothesis of equal population proportions were true, how much difference between the sample proportions would we expect from sampling variation alone?

So:

Confidence interval → keep proportions separate.


Hypothesis test under \(H_0:p_1=p_2\) → pool the proportions.

title: 8  Inference for Categorical Data
text:
30.1 Independent Observations
Observations should contribute independently.
For example, each visitor should contribute one independent observation rather than the same visitor appearing repeatedly and being treated as independent observations.
A huge dataset does not solve a violation of independence.

More rows do not fix dependence among observations.

title: 8  Inference for Categorical Data
text:
30.2 Mutually Exclusive Categories
Each observational unit should contribute to exactly one cell.
For example, a visitor cannot simultaneously be classified as both:

Purchased
Did not purchase

The categories must be mutually exclusive for the table being analyzed.

text:
30.3 Expected Counts
Expected counts should be sufficiently large for the chi-square approximation to be reliable.
A simple conservative rule is:
\[
\boxed{
E_{ij}\geq5
}
\]
for every cell.

A statistically significant association does not automatically establish causality.
Ask:

How were the data generated?

Random assignment can support causal interpretation.
Observational association by itself cannot.
